en: Kauthuma Gṛhyasūtra 1:
Now, therefore, the expiations.

Now, therefore, I shall describe the sequence of rites: whether one is a householder or a student (brahmacārī), the householder performs the rite in the domestic fire (gṛhyāgni), while the student performs it in the common fire (laukikāgni). If the service is performed according to the *iṣṭicaraṇa* [tradition], or if the period of studentship has been interrupted, the occasional rite (*naimittika*) must be performed in the common fire, preceded by the morning oblation.

In the case of re-consecration (*punarādheya*), one should avoid performing it starting from the evening; however, if there is the occurrence of an immediate expiation (*tātkālika-prāyaścitta*), then the rite should be performed with those two [offerings].

If the full-moon oblation (*paurṇamāsī-āhuti*) has passed, they should perform that specific rite with those two; if it was the new-moon day (*parvan*), it should be performed after making a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). In the absence of that, one should perform it immediately. On the other hand, the expiation for the new-moon day consists of three nights or five nights, beginning from the preceding night.

One should perform both sacrifices preceded by expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Having resolved upon those two festival days (*parvan*), if one has passed them, one should likewise perform those two offerings (*iṣṭi*). In that case, if there is an omission or if the time has elapsed, they should perform the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) for the sake of expiation; or else, after that, a *Prājāpatya* sacrifice. Furthermore, regarding the specific rule concerning the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*), if one should touch it within the ritual enclosure (*tantra*).

One or both of them should perform [the rite] for the mantras; he should speak those two [verses], and taking the sacrificial grass (samidh) joined with the lute (tantrī), they should then perform the ritual of ascending anew and the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma).

Having silently sprinkled [water] around and having offered the oblation (āhuti) with the mantra, the one who is not the priest (anarthastara) should place the two pieces of sacrificial wood (samidh) upon the fire and recite the mantra for the act of shouting (bhaṣat-karma).

In this case, it is the same whether the *pup* (the fire-drill) or the wife should perform the silent re-ascension (*samāropaṇa*); they should perform it as something to be done. Or rather, it is said that this should be done by oneself; then, from that point onward, there would be a distinction: in another fire, one should personally perform the re-ascension of the fires belonging to us, and likewise in the sacrifice (*yajña*), one should perform the re-ascension.
Having performed the initial re-ascension and having released the cord from that [fire], one should say: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ."

Standing silently, one should not depart; if that [fire] reaches the wife’s fire, the ritual is ruined. One should personally perform the expiation in one's own domestic fire (*svagṛhyāgni*). From this point forward, there shall be a distinction: if there was no formal installation (*anāropaṇa*), then the installation (*samāropaṇa*) should be performed according to the rules for clarified butter (*ājyatantra*).
Starting again from the beginning, if any ritual—from the *prāyaścitti-homa* up to the *prapada*—has been omitted, [it must be restored].

Some say that if the morning oblation has been omitted, there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*); for the omission of rites and so forth, there is a repetition [of the rite], and after the principal part (*pradhāna*), there is expiation. Beyond this, the specific details are explained according to the ritual manual (*tantra*): on a site sloping toward the east or the north, one should smear a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) there. (Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra 1)
Kauthuma Gṛhyasūtra 2:

Now, therefore, having turned toward the east and sat down loudly with the syllable *oṃ* upon *darbha* grass whose tips point north, he should then have the tracing performed while looking at the domestic fire.

Having offered the morning oblation therein, he should obtain a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas; in the absence of such a person, the rule regarding the *khādira* [wood] applies, as well as the *chatra* and *uttarāsaṃ*; some say that the *khādira* is the *nyā*, and thus he should entreat the Brāhmaṇa.

The Brāhmaṇa should say, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ; Bṛhaspati is the Brahman, I am the human. The teacher should give him two *darbha* blades. The Brāhmaṇa should cast away [the blades] with the words, "Nirastaḥ parāvasuḥ," and having strewn *darbha* grass with tips pointing eastward for the sake of a seat, he should sit facing north with the mantra, "I sit in the seat of Vasu," pronouncing "Om" in a low voice. Then the teacher, having honored the Brāhmaṇa...

Taking a bronze vessel or an unbaked earthen vessel—excluding copper—and silver, he should take rice grains with a new winnowing basket, carry them out toward the north, and fill the vessel once for the purpose of the pouring-out (nirvāpa). He should do this twice silently. Saying, "I shall sprinkle," he pours water forward; then, having carried it out toward the north, he proceeds with the sweeping and so forth according to the ritual procedure for clarified butter (ājya-tantra).

Regarding what is prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras: one should perform the rite of the nine joints; having raised that vessel and placed it in the middle of the fire, one should say, "Let there be an offering.
Then, one should cook the living rice grains.
Having sprinkled them with the *sruva* ladle and moved them from the fire onto the sacrificial grass at its northern end, one should sprinkle them again.
Then, having taken the fuel, there is a specific rule regarding the sacrificial wood (*samidh*):
the followers of the Ṛgveda sacrifice with *khadira* wood; the Bodhāyanas [also] with *palāśa*; and the followers of the Sāmaveda sacrifice with *udumbara*.
Having had them prepared to be a span (*prādeśa*) long, with backs like a hair, straight at the top, with a thickness equal to the joint of a thumb, and with their tips clearly marked;

In the absence of that, having taken seventeen *darbha* blades— one for the *anaṣṭa-artham*, one for the *prapada-artham*, and fifteen for the *idhma-artham*— and having poured clarified butter over them with the *sruva* spoon, he should set aside the tip, the middle, and the root for the sake of the subsequent offerings (*anuyāja*) on the north side; then, having thrown the fifteen blades into the fire, he should mutter the *prapada* formula with the remainder, beginning with "yāvacīri" and ending with "śaṭha," as far as the word "svāhā."

Maintaining the forms, having offered oblations into the fire that destroys forms, one should worship with the remaining unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). Then, having offered with the three *vyāhṛtis*, and then having offered the *kāmajā-vyāhṛti*, one should offer the "two eyes" using four portions (*caturgṛhīta*) with the *sruva* ladle. Regarding these, it should be according to the purpose in the *Carutantra*; however, the specific procedure for the granting of boons (*varadāna*) is stated therein.
And according to the principle of the *khādira* [wood], having stated that the *kauthuma* is mentioned in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*, the *kauthuma* follows the path of the *kuthuma*. (KauthGS 2)
Kauthuma Gṛhyasūtra 3:

Now, therefore, having inspected the vessel for the *caru*, it should be placed facing [the performer]; some say it should be placed facing north. It should be made in two parts for the sake of the *caru*. Having set down the *sruva* ladle, which has a hole at its tip, in its absence a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*) may be used.

Or, having sprinkled clarified butter over it in the middle, having once taken a portion from the eastern part of the sacrificial oblation (*caru*), and having taken a second portion from the middle, and having again sprinkled butter over the remainder in the *sruva* ladle, one should offer it in the middle of the fire. If there is a second [portion], one should take a single portion from the western part of the *caru*, sprinkle butter over it twice, and offer it in the north-eastern direction. If it belongs to the Jāmadagnyas, [the portions] should be taken from the middle, the back, and the front.

Having cut off [the portion] once with a *bhṛgu*-shaped blade, a *caru* of those [grains] that have been parched is prepared there in a *kārṣmarya* vessel. One should remove the embers with the verse "With the vigor of you two... He should perform this twice silently. If the ritual action is struck by the fires, he should offer the *prājāpatya* expiation.

If it has been passed over or interrupted, having offered oblations to the sixty deities at that very moment, he should perform the rites for the *dravasaurya* offerings throughout that elapsed day and night.

If it should become necessary to perform a rite in the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*) on a festival day (*parvan*) or similar occasion, or if one wishes to perform a ritual, then—provided that the fourth day after the onset of menstruation has passed and no *caṇḍāla* has entered—the penance consists of shaving the head according to the *kṛcchra* rule; such is the penance.
Thus ends the penance. (Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra 3)
Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra 4:

Now, regarding the expiation for a festival (parvan): whether during the northern course of the sun or the southern course, in the spring and other seasons, in the sixth month, or in the four months of the lunar and solar cycles—on these occasions, if an expiation should be performed in the midst of a desired sacrifice to Agni at the beginning of a festival, it is to be done in the domestic fire (gṛhyāgni).

Even if the time for the ritual action (*karma*) falls on the fourth day of the lunar fortnight, starting from that day, let it not reach its conclusion; rather, the performance should take place in the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire, and it must be performed with the formal resolutions (*saṃkalpa*) regarding the month and so forth. If there is an expiation (*prāyaścitti*) in the marriage ceremony, and if it occurs in the first half of the month, it should begin on the following full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*).

It should be performed with the resolutions for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. Regarding the statement "two *iṣṭis* [are required] for the *viṣṭi*," in that context, the second *viṣṭi* refers to the day.
In the sacrifice, there is misfortune; therefore, an obstacle (*vighna*) should be created by those two for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitti*).

One should perform it with three *avamāra* verses beginning with "tāṃ svadhā me. If it should occur in the middle of the *iṣṭi*, the expiation should be performed; [this applies] in the interval between the two *āghāra* offerings and during an eclipse (*rāhu-parvan*), as it is said regarding the *aindrapamāha*.
Having stated that for the first *paṅkti* and the second [verse] in the *gāyatrī* meter, the deity of both is the Moon (*candra*), one should perform the expiation (*prāyaścitti*).

If, on the full-moon day (*parvan*), there is a verse addressed to Sūrya (*saurya*) such as "The bright face of the gods" (*citram devānām*) or "Upwards that [face]" (*udu tyam*), whether it be in the *triṣṭubh* or *gāyatrī* meter, having stated that the deity of both is Sūrya, one should perform the expiation. If one performs the rite again without having performed the expiation, [the following applies].

An expiation (prāyaścitti) must be performed; having resolved upon it in the midst of the Śrāddha rites, there the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa) or the offering into the hand (kapāṇi-huta) should likewise be performed while eating, and an expiation must be performed. Furthermore, regarding specific rules for husband and wife, if menstruation occurs or if one has approached a Caṇḍāla in the interval between the two, an expiation must be performed; [likewise] in the interval between their establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna), in the heap [of ashes], or in the interval, [there is] the cessation of contact.

Or if an increase [of the period] should occur, an expiation must be performed. Between those two [periods], having entered another village and traveled along the road, an expiation must be performed. Between those two, if both [periods] occur, or if there is intercourse during the day, an expiation must be performed. A man, while in the midst of eating, likewise having engaged in the act of intercourse, or having been touched by a dog or a cat—[an expiation must be performed].

An expiation must be performed; furthermore, there is a specific rule for those who maintain the domestic fire (*gṛhya-agni*) and for widows who do not maintain the fire. Having touched a widow, an expiation must be performed.

[The following acts require expiation: eating the food of a *śūdra*, being a follower of the Cārvāka school, approaching the wife of another, abandoning one’s own duty, constantly eating the food of others, likewise being a non-recipient of gifts (*anagrāha*), killing a cow or a Brahmin, being a householder who eats the food of a prostitute, and abandoning the study of the scriptures.

One who corrupts sacred knowledge, one who speaks ill of preceptors, one who destroys living beings, one who eats the leavings of a cat, one who sells the Vedas, one who defiles a maiden or a devoted wife,

one who abandons his own family, one who reviles a teacher or a preceptor, one who approaches the wife of a preceptor, one who eats meat, one who neglects the time for *śrāddha* rites, as well as one who eats at a *śrāddha*, one who destroys a pond, one who is a year-old [animal], one who is lustful toward his own wife, one who strikes a Brahmin, and one who strikes with earth or stones.
Those who have spat upon the virtuous or defiled Brahmins are equal to Caṇḍālas. If they touch the domestic fire, the couple must perform the purification of their dwelling and clothing;
for the sake of expiation, the sixty deities have been mentioned.

The rites beginning with *kanyahṛti* should be performed with the three *vyāhṛtis*; this repetition should be done again with the three [mantras] twelve times over, and the *prājāpatya* penance must be performed.
One does not [perform] the end of the five together—[with the verses] "Protect us with thy foremost power" (RV 8.61.13–15), one [offering] for Prajāpati;

and that which is the loan [of the Soma], ending with the fourth [verse] as the *sviṣṭakṛt*—this is the expiation for these. Thus, he who knows the various expiations according to the Brāhmaṇa is liberated from the body; he who is liberated from the body [is truly free]. 4. Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra.
Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra 5:

Now, therefore, follows the expiation for transpositions. In all cases, there is the sprinkling with water, the Prājāpatya offering, and the Yatkusīda offering. Having completed these, and having offered the Arghya-Śabalihoma, if there was a transposition at the beginning, one should offer the Yatkusīda; [and] whatever is not performed everywhere, that too is clarified butter for the consecratory rites.
Having offered for the sacrificer, it becomes a *tatanūṣa*; that sacrifice without a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for a Brāhmaṇa becomes Rākṣasa.

He who sacrifices without this [fee] falls into hell; both the sacrificer and the Brāhmaṇa [are lost]. By neglecting the time for every oblation, the Brāhmaṇa becomes a destroyer of the sacrifice; by neglecting the three [daily] junctions (*saṃdhyā*), he becomes a destroyer of the Veda; by neglecting the time of the twilight, the Brāhmaṇa becomes a destroyer of light.

In all cases, one who studies during forbidden times (*pradoṣa*) is a killer of the Veda; one of another caste who imparts knowledge is a killer of the Guru; and one who habitually abandons [his duties] at will is a killer of his father. These are the names for those who have fallen from their state. One should not speak with them, nor greet them, nor look upon them on the road. If one has done so through negligence, one should mutter the *Gāyatrī* eight times. (Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra 5)
Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra 6:
The conjunction of two wives with the fire.
Now, therefore, if among all castes there is a case where Brāhmaṇas again exercise lordship [over the household], one should first lead forth half of the domestic fire.

For the purpose of joining those two, on the fourth day, the sacrificer, having commenced in the evening and performed the descent (*avarohaṇa*) into the eastern fire, prepares a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) there; having established the fire with the three-verse hymn beginning "Agni, you who increase" (*agniṃ vo vṛdhantam*), he immediately takes his wife by the hand over the new fire with a vessel and joins her with the three-verse hymn beginning "This praise-song" (*imaṃ stomam*). At the end of each verse, he pronounces four syllables in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).

Then, after the clarified butter has been offered with the six verses beginning with "Then let Agni come," he should cause the sacrificer to recite [the mantra] while performing breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Having sprinkled water around [the fire], he offers oblations saying, "To Agni, svāhā!

To Prajāpati, svāhā! Having sprinkled water around again, he should consign the fire into the kindling wood (*samāropaṇa*) while singing the *Vāmadevya* chant. If he is in another country, he should perform the rite there in a common (*laukika*) fire as before; having joined [the fires] as previously described, if there is a specific rule regarding the lordship of the beloved (*apriyādhipatya*), we shall explain that therein.

Having invited the Brahmins, and having eaten a hundred cakes and a meal, he bathed, adorned himself, took water in his water-pot, and went into the middle of a forest. In that place, having observed a branch of the *arka* tree that was not withered, tender, possessed of auspicious leaves, fruit-bearing, wide-spreading, full of sap, and endowed with these qualities; and having deliberated upon a Veda-knowing Brahmin for the sake of his father, he caused him to bathe at the *arka* branch.

One should not take [the girl] without having clothed her with new garments. The Brāhmaṇa, standing before the bridegroom while preparing a sacrificial mound (sthāṇḍila), recites "devasya tvā" and says, "I accept the gift of the Arka-maiden. Having sat down to the north of the Arka tree, the Brāhmaṇa, being heated by the sun, wraps an Arka branch around himself.
Then all [those present], facing either east or north, honor the Brāhmaṇa; thereafter, ten cakes (apūpa) are offered to each one.

Having placed the remainder to the north, he should establish the common fire (*laukikāgni*). Then, having performed the rites from the sweeping of the ground up to the *prapada* offering, and having offered the fuel-sticks (*idhmāṅga*), he should then offer with the three *vyāhṛtis*. Next, he offers with the six verses beginning with "Agniretu" and again with the three [verses].
Then the sacrificer, standing, circumambulates the fire while holding it; [the thought is]: "Agni is the Sun; all Brāhmaṇas are contained within him."

Having spoken thus, he should silently circumambulate [the fire] three times from left to right; then, sitting in his own place, he should take up the *sahitāra* with his right hand, reciting "tad gṛhṇāmi te" in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). Having completed the subsequent oblation (*totopariṣṭāhoma*), he should give ten portions of the remaining cakes (*apūpa*) to the *brahmán* priest and consume ten himself. There, having sprinkled water around the fire and worshipped it with the *vyāhṛti*s.

One should offer clarified butter with three [verses]; having released that, then the Vāmadevya [chant], the benedictory words of the Brahmins, and the girl should go to the house; then again the lordship, again the lordship. (Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra 6)
Kauthuma Gṛhyasūtra 7:

Now follows the examination of the proper time for conception. From the onset of the first menses, having bathed and become pure, he should perform the recitation of auspicious verses (*svastivācana*), decorate the bedchamber, scatter flowers and fruits, adorn it with lamps in every direction, and prepare a long square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with fragrant clay.

Having spread a mat of *uparīkṣapa* grass with its tips pointing north, and then having spread a new cloth upon it with its ends pointing east, he should have his wife lie down with her head toward the east. Then, facing upward, he should press his knees and feet against the earth and, standing near her and facing her, mutter the mantra "May Viṣṇu prepare the womb" (*viṣṇur yoniṃ kalpayatu*) eight times while touching her two thighs with joined hands. [This is done] for the sake of obtaining eight sons.
If the husband is unavailable at the time of her season, she must not approach another man; the period of the season lasts for six nights.
Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra 8:
Now follows the consecration of the embryo. On the sixth day after sexual intercourse, beginning from that day, on every even day among the even nights, a son should be born;
on odd nights, daughters would be born—knowing this, when the bride’s first pregnancy occurs...

For the sake of purifying the child who is to be born through the purification of the mother's womb, one should perform the *puṃsavana* and *sīmantonnayana* rites; having counted one month from whichever day the conception occurs, the third month is auspicious. Then, on the preceding day, the *nāndīmukha* rite is performed; thereafter, on the following day at dawn, having bathed, [one prepares] a quadrangular [altar].

Having smeared the sacrificial ground and sat down upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing north, the wife to the south and the sacrificer to the north, the Brahmin sits facing north. Then, either with or without the formal leading forward (*praṇayana*) of the fire, having offered the morning oblation, having offered from the sweeping up (*samūhana*) until the end of the foot-steps, and having offered a portion of the fuel-wood (*idhmāṅga*), he then offers with the three *vyāhṛti*s. Thereafter, the sacrificer stands behind his wife.

One should touch the navel of the bridegroom, beginning from the right side; one should say, "It shall be a male. Then, having sat in his own place and completed the *homa* thereafter, the sacrificer (yajamāna), after the bride has bathed again, places twenty-one flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and barley grains in a new winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), takes them, and departs from the village.
Having gone near the king of banyan trees (*vaṭarāja*) and approached the goddess Vāsinī there, he recites the verse beginning with "utsāhavyāpinī" [in the *adrime*].

"Grant me that prosperity which I desire and which is ever-present; therefore, fulfill my wish. Having worshipped with flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), having scattered barley over it, and having cut a branch with its tips pointing northward using an axe, he should take it either to a place of herbs or into the open air.
Then, bringing it into the house with its tips pointing upward, he should install it upon his own seat in the middle of the storehouse or in the vicinity of the water-jar (*maṇika*).

Then, having smeared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), he should say: "What is sought? Having performed [the rite] up to the end of the *prapada* formula, having offered the fuel-wood (*idhma*) portions, and having again offered with the three *vyāhṛti*s, he should have seven parts of that herb ground by a maiden with brothers who faces east; while she is bringing it back, he should murmur over that established [substance] the *navavaḥ saśrinan akṣi* mantra, and then take hold of it.

The sacrificer then satisfies [the fire]. Behind the fire, the wife lies down facing east with her head toward the north; between the fire and the wife, the sacrificer lies down facing west. With the mantra "punānāgnih," he squeezes the flour-liquid into his right nostril, then, having squeezed out the flour, places it in water and gives the cloth to the Brahman priest; he should place that liquid in the bellies of both of them.
Then, having sat down in his own place and completed that which follows, there is the feeding of Brāhmaṇas; then the feeding of Brāhmaṇas. (KauthGS 8)
Kauthuma Gṛhyasūtra 9:

Now, in the fourth month, the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) is to be performed. On the preceding day, the Nāndīmukha rite is performed; then, on the following day at dawn, having bathed, the sacrificer brings a branch of the Udumbara tree into the house in the prescribed manner, along with a porcupine quill marked with three white spots.
Having cooked rice mixed with sesame seeds on a common fire and placed it to the north of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), he performs the rites up to the *prapada* as before;
having offered the fuel-wood portions and again offered with the three *vyāhṛti*s, the sacrificer, standing behind [the fire],
takes hold of it, mutters the *ūrjaṃ tvā* formula, and then, looking at the tip of his nose, raises it up to the level of his forehead.

Having established it with the mantra "yenīditā," and having grasped it again with a porcupine quill while reciting "rākā" (according to some teachers), he establishes it. Having performed the sprinkling three times silently, he sits down in his own place. Then, having completed the oblations from above, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite, "O Vadhū, holding the vessel of clarified butter, what do you see? After singing the Vāmadevya Sāman, there follows the feeding of the Brahmins; then the feeding of the Brahmins. (Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra 9)

KauthGS 10: Now, at the time of a son's birth, beginning with the *soṣyantī-homa*, having performed the partial carrying forward of the fire (*ekadeśapraṇayana*), bathed, smeared the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*),

and completed the rites from the sweeping (*samūhana*) up to the *prapada* offering, and having offered the fuel-wood (*idhma*), he then offers clarified butter with the two verses beginning "yātiraśvī" at the time of the head's birth.

Having offered the oblation, he should utter the name "Śabda. Or rather, O best of sages, the son should begin: "I ask you, O friend, out of affection; therefore, before the taking of the [sacred] thread, how were the names previously established? Tell me that truly and in its entirety. We shall explain this without omission: one should perform this rite of naming after the ceremony of the sacred thread (*upanayana*); if it is done otherwise through delusion or error, it is as if not done at all.

This is offered for me; therefore, people say that where there is non-existence, one should offer an expiation for it. Having offered [the oblation] at the end of the birth-rite, while mentally intending "O Śabda, O Viṣṇuprada Devaśarman," he should cause the *mānasa* [name] to enter.

At the end of the dispute, he should speak the name of the *viśvavādya*. What indeed is his name? At the end of the *śabda*, a name based on a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) should be made, or else "Magha."
If, because the two sons were carried in one vehicle, the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) and other sacraments were not performed, then after the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*),

he himself should perform the sacraments separately for each. Having said, "I shall describe the birth-rite," and having placed [the child] on the lap according to the rule "at ten nights," he should [offer] thirty-three grains [of rice] with honey and clarified butter, one by one.

Taking a palmful [of grain] and joining it together on both sides with the formula "Thou art glory, glory," he should grasp it along with a piece of gold using his two thumbs and two ring fingers; or, in their absence, with *kuśa* grass. Then, mixing barley-flour with the two kinds of clarified butter, he should give it to the child to eat with the formulas "May the gods...
and "Medhām te..."; thereafter follows the sacrificial fee for the Brahmins.
Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra 11:
Thereafter, [the rite] is performed at the first appearance of the moon.

From the birth onwards, after ten nights—or two [fortnights]—under that same lunar mansion, one should look at that boy, whether he is still in the womb or already born, for the first time after he has emerged from the water.
Having performed the visualization of their absence, one should prepare the *cāma* offering. How shall I explain it? On the previous day, one should perform the *nāndīmukha* rite;

then, on the following morning, having bathed, the sacrificer should smear a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), divide a portion of the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*), and having performed the rites from the sweeping of the ground up to the *prapada*, he should offer the fuel-wood (*idhma*). Then the mother, taking her own son, [should dress him] in an unwashed garment.

Having enclosed [the fire] on the south side, having sat down facing west, having performed that [rite], and having handed it into the hand of the husband, she should go behind him, sit down to the north, look at her son belonging to the sacrificer, offer oblations with the three *vyāhṛtis*, and handing it back again, the sacrificer should touch his two eyes from the middle of the five [limbs] with the two verses beginning "Who are you? and "Which one...? for the sake of protection.
With the four-syllabled "Sī," he should touch both ears; with the three-syllabled "Eṣo 'si," the tip of the nose and the base of the middle finger;

with the four-syllabled "Amṛto 'si," he should touch each of the hands and arms individually; having touched each of the hands and arms individually with the four-syllabled "Amṛto 'si," he should grasp the head with the remainder [of the formula], and then the mother [should do so] with her left hand.

Taking a *kumāryavaka* (a young shoot), he should whisper the previously mentioned narrative into the right ear; then the sacrificer should take hold of it. Then, in a whisper, he should utter the name "Hetyativādanīya" (the one to be addressed beyond the call). Thereafter, having completed the oblation and sung the *Vāmadevya*, and having caused [the sacrificer] to recite the benedictions for the husband's return, the feeding of the Brahmins should be performed in the same manner. KauthGS 11.5–6.
Kauthuma Gṛhyasūtra 12:

Now, therefore, follows the worship of the Moon. It should be performed on the third, fifth, seventh, or eighth day of the bright fortnight, beginning with the new moon; it is to be carried out in the third or sixth month on a day purified by the five-fold examination.

Having invited a *chandoga* Brahmin learned in the Vedas— a true Brahmin who has risen from his seat— the host should go out from the village, place him with his head facing east, and, being able, take a golden vessel or one of bell-metal (avoiding clay), step into the water knee-deep,
fill it with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and having drawn it up with the mantra "śanno devīḥ," he should place it upon the head [of the guest] with the words "addhṛtyam. He who...

Having emerged from the water with the *pāvamānī* verses, one should enter the village with the *vāmadevya* hymn. In all cases, there should be no conversation and no offering of food; having become well-composed, one should place that water-vessel on a seat near the house of the sacrificer, near an assembly of gods, or in the midst of a cow-pen, covering it above with *kuśa* grass. While the Brahmins, the sacrificer, and others are eating or departing, these [verses] are recited.
Having established the *ahassahasira* until sunset, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) should go out from his house,

smear a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in a pure place, face south, enter the circle with the mantra "Hā u ya candra," sit facing east, perform the recitation for well-being (*svastivācana*), fill the hands of the sacrificer with a handful of flowers, and stand facing the moon.

Then the mother, having lifted up the boy, turns toward the south facing westward, hands the boy into the other's hands, and goes behind to stand on the north side. While the sacrificer holds the boy over a handful of flowers, she pays homage with the three verses beginning "O thou of very gentle mind," and having handed him back to the mother facing northward, he should form a hollowed palm (añjali) with both hands; [he should offer] that añjali.

Having filled [the vessel] with the *brahmapraṇava*, if there is a verse, he should pour it out with joined palms; then, having again filled it silently, and likewise having poured it out twice silently, sitting down facing west and having sung the *Vāmadevya*, then follows the feeding of the Brahmins—then the feeding of the Brahmins. (Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra 12)
Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra 13:

In the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) is performed as an auspicious rite (*abhyudayika*). On the preceding day, on the following day, or at dawn, the sacrificer, having bathed, cooks either barley flour or milk-rice (*pāyasa*)—prepared without rice grains according to the ritual procedure or its omission—and [the child's] father and mother [partake of it].

And having taken the boy and sat down, he should perform the birth-rite (jātakarma); at the commencement of the rite, he should eat milk-rice (pāyasa), and then there is the feeding of Brahmins; then the feeding of Brahmins. (Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra 13)
Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra 14:

In the third year, the shaving ceremony should be performed. On the preceding day, the rite for prosperity (*ābhyudayika*) is performed; then, on the following morning, having bathed, the sacrificer, having smeared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and having placed the clarified butter to the south of the circular area, starting from the southeast (*āgneya*); [he proceeds].

The barber, having sat facing the east, then [offers] warm water for the journey; thereafter, having bathed him with Darbha grass and a bunch of Piñjūlī on the north of the sacrificial mound or in the north-western direction, and having performed the worldly rites with red bull-dung, rice-and-pulse porridge (kṛsara), and a sthālīpāka cooked as a common meal, he should not perform the homa in the place where the name is assigned; then, having established the Gṛhya fire.

Having offered the morning oblation, one should have the hair of those belonging to the forest-clans (*vanya-gotra*) shaved entirely or in part; some [should have] three tufts (*tri-śikhā*), others five tufts (*pañca-śikhā*), according to the custom of their respective clans and families. They should bury the hair in the forest; some, however, place it down [in a pit]. Then the youth (*māṇavaka*), having bathed again, and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), having sat down in his own place, should complete the subsequent rite, sing the *Vāmadevya* chant, and thereafter provide a feast for the Brahmins.
Then follows the feeding of the Brahmins. (Kauthuma Gṛhyasūtra 14)

In the eighth year, before the completion of twelve years, one should undertake the life of a student (*brahmacarya*). On that eighth year, having commenced on an auspicious lunar mansion as prescribed in the Smṛtis during the forenoon of that day, one should first perform the *nāndīmukha* rite and then [proceed] on a day of merit (*puṇyāha*).

Having commenced in the forenoon and facing the east, then on an auspicious day in the forenoon, the teacher, having bathed with *sahasarasa* [water], having caused the student (*vaṭu*) to perform a full ablution, and having himself bathed and adorned himself, having dressed him in a new garment, having smeared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*),
and having sat down facing the east while treading upon the foot-washing stone, the student likewise [stands] to the south of the teacher.
He himself should give [the garment] made of wood, or silently [give] a new one to the one who has taken the vow; likewise with gold, [he gives it] upon hair and upon skin.

Having become one wearing the sacred thread (*upavīta*), having sipped water (*ācamana*) again for both of them, and having established the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*), [he performs the rite]. For those whose lineage (*gotra*) is forgotten, [the procedure is as follows]:

at the tonsure (*caula*), the initiation (*upanayana*), and the godāna, having performed from the sweeping of the ground (*samūhana*) up to the *prapada* offering, and having offered the fuel-wood (*idhma*), then, while she holds on to him, [he offers] with the *vyāhṛti* formulas.
Having offered three oblations and taken hold of the young student with both hands, he should make him recite "Yama mā dabhat.

Then, meditating on Savitṛ, he should look at him; saying "nuṣṇena," he should sprinkle warm water while meditating on Vāyu. The young student, having filled his right hand in the *añjali* gesture and having had the hair on the right side shaved with the mantra "apa undantu," [the teacher] should shave it with "viṣṇordaṣṭro..."

Saying, "If [it is] in the mirror, O herb, protect him," he washes a tuft of *darbha* grass, establishes it in its place, and says over the mirror, "O axe, do not harm him. Having joined the herbs with the words "O herbs," the learned men should sprinkle him with the verse beginning "With which Pūṣan.
Another person, having once cut the tips of seven hairs joined with the tips of *darbha* grass using an iron blade, [should do so] silently for the ox.

Having thrown [the water] again, starting from the sprinkling (*undana*) and so forth, and having thus subsequently grasped the head of the northern [fire] with the formula "The three-fold life-span," he should murmur it; having approached that, he should say to the Brāhmaṇa, "Let him do it. The teacher should ask, "What is his name?
The disciple should state the constellation and his own name himself, while the disciple remains silent, hidden in the *añjali* [of his hands], and likewise on the ground. Then the teacher—

He should say [the mantra]; with those two hands, he should take the *añjali* of the student. The preceptor, facing east, standing behind the student who is also facing east, holding the mantra "devasya tvā," and having touched the region of the student's navel with the palms of both hands, [recites] up to the end of "prāṇānām" [and then touches] the heart with "ka ity adara" and "ahura" [and then] with "kṛsara."

[The teacher] places [the fuel-stick] on the neck with the formula "To the God thee," with the left hand for the left [hand], or with the right hand for the left [hand] while the thread is over the right shoulder; then with the formula "To Prajāpati thee.
Then the student, facing east, [is addressed by] the teacher: "O Brahmacārin, so-and-so, place this fuel-stick [on the fire]; drink water; perform your duties;
do not sleep during the day"—meaning that you are a Brahmacārin. Perform your own fire-rites, [and] rinse your mouth.

Or [the teacher] may say, "The lineage-fire is the breath," or "The stomach is the fire"; having instructed them, saying, "It should be done thus," and they having replied, "So be it," he should offer the morning oblation, sing his own hymn (*sūkta*), perform breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and— whether in his own lineage (*svagotra*) or another’s lineage (*anyagotra*)—
having distributed the portion for the Vedic seers (*vedarya-bhāga*) among those of his own lineage or others as appropriate, he should place it before those of his own lineage.

Having declared "the *śāuda* [fire] is in one place," they know that the leading forth (*praṇayana*) of that fire takes place; having immediately placed that fire upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*),

and having performed the rites from the sweeping (*samūhana*) up to the *prapada*, and having offered the fuel-wood (*idhma*) portion, and then, while the student holds on, having offered with the three *vyāhṛtis* and again with all of them together, and having the student offer with the formulas beginning "O Agni, Lord of Vows" (*agne vratapate*), he should lead the student between the fire and the teacher.

Having reflected thus, O Brāhmaṇa, the teacher should stand facing the east; having stood before the Brāhmaṇa who is also facing east upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward, he should fill [the vessel] and take hold of a water-pot. Having caused the disciple to form the *añjali* gesture, and having filled the Brāhmaṇa’s hands in the *añjali* gesture while the teacher looks on, the teacher should mutter the mantra and cause the disciple’s joined palms to behold it. Then the student should perform *prāṇāyāma*.

Having performed the sprinkling and worship, one should take a single fuel-stick with the mantra "To Agni, a fuel-stick" (*agnaye samidham*). Having offered a second [stick] mentally to Prajāpati, and having honored oneself by standing before the fire with the mantra "May faith be mine" (*śraddhā me dhāḥ*), one should take ashes with the mantra "The triple life-span" (*triyāyuṣam*).

Having rubbed them together with the middle, ring, and thumb fingers, one should apply them to the forehead with the mantra "Brahmā, you are a drop" (*brahmā bindurasi*) and to the head with the mantra "Life, you are a drop" (*āyuḥ bindurasi*).

With the mantra "Śrīr bindur asi," he should apply [the water] to the chest; with "Śraddhā bindur asi," to the throat; with "Medhā bindur asi," to the navel; with "Tejo bindur asi," to the root of the right arm; with "Kāma bindur asi," to the left arm; and with "Vāsu pṛṣṭhe sarvakāma," to all the limbs. Then he should beg for alms, and give that alms-food to the Brahman priest. Remaining under the authority of his teacher, he should stand silently. Then, at midday, he should perform the ritual purification (mārjana) as previously described.
One should perform the fire-rite in the evening; thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins—thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins. // KauthGS 15 //
Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra 16:
Now, having sat down in his own place, the teacher shall announce the ritual for the gift of the cow (*godāna*). Likewise, the Brāhmaṇa [acting as] Brahman sits between the fire and the teacher;
the student, following the teacher, sits upon the tips of the *darbha* grass with his right knee bent, and the teacher [takes] the girdle (*mekhalā*).

Having tied [the girdle] three times around and having caused the student (māṇavaka) to sip water while reciting the mantra "iyam duruktāt," the teacher sips water again. Then the student, becoming resplendent like Garuda, at an auspicious moment, during the mutual initiation (upanayana), sits down before the teacher. Thereafter, having completed the oblation (homa), the imparting of the Sāvitrī follows in the midst [of the rite].
Having uttered the *praṇava*, he should pause at each foot [of the verse]; likewise, pausing at the second [foot], he should then pause at the third, preceded by the *praṇava*.

Having caused him to recite each of the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by *om*, and then having loudly uttered "om," the teacher should murmur, "O you of good fame, [make me] of good fame! and, saying "O you of great fame, [make me] of good fame! he should cause the student to take hold of a staff made of *pālāśa* wood.
Then, with his right hand, he should take two fuel-sticks, saying: "Dharma is, Dharma is. (KauthGS 16)
Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra 17:

Now, therefore, regarding expiations: for a householder or a student who has drunk liquor, had sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍāla woman, committed incest with the teacher’s wife, killed a Brahmin, slaughtered a cow, stolen gold, accepted improper gifts, or eaten another's food—for the sake of removing such lightness of fault, the expiation for a Brāhmaṇa is the Hittīrtha.

Saying "I shall speak," one should observe a three-night fast; then, having cooked sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and having caused the shaving of the head, one should take auspiciously-cut water, bathe [the person] at a river, and take black cow-dung. Reciting, "Born and situated in the heart of the cow, you have purified the world; therefore, having become a purifier, effect the destruction of all sins," one should take that cow-dung, mix it with water, and [place it] upon a *pālāśa* leaf.

Having taken twelve portions, having filled [the vessel], and having consecrated it with a hundred prostrations, one should smear it on the head. One should perform three *homa* offerings extending from the *brahman* priest to the *agnidhra*; this is practiced everywhere. As before, there is the purification of the offered oblation (*upahṛta-pāvana*) and a further repetition. For the student (*brahmacārī*), there is the drinking of wine and the tasting of honey; every night, he is not free from [these]. He should not wear the sacred thread (*upavīta*), nor be naked (*digambara*). He must guard the door and avoid chewing betel nut (*kramuka*). Sexual intercourse during the day is prohibited.

Furthermore, regarding eating during the day, conversing with outcasts (caṇḍāla), lying to others, eating the leftovers of others, consuming food at the *pārvaṇa* rite, and performing the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* or *ekoddiṣṭa* rites—one must observe celibacy (*brahmacarya*) in these instances because they are complete [in their requirements]. It is known from the *Dharmakti* that through negligence there is lightness [of the penance]; one should not perform it if it lacks its essence, for it becomes ineffective. Therefore, one devoted to dharma should constantly practice the recitation of the *kusuma-grantha*.

Having become thus, he should cause the two of them to sip water again; having performed the rite down to the *prapada* [foot-washing], and having offered a portion of the fuel-sticks (*idhmāṅga*), the teacher should then, while the student has touched him from behind, offer oblations with the three *vyāhṛtis* and the five beginning with "O Agni, [guard] the vows" (*agne vratapate*).

Having caused the student to recite the mantra, the teacher, standing in his own place, and the young student, facing east, should have him take up water for the *udbhava* rite and form a hollowed palm (*añjali*) toward the Brahman.

Having filled [the vessel] and recited the mantra beginning with *ā gantreṇa*, the teacher should look at the joined palms of the disciples and ask in his mind, "What is your name? The disciples should whisper their names based on the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) under which they were born. Then, having seated them in their respective places and completed the subsequent fire-oblation (*homa*), for the purpose of bestowing the *Sāvitrī* mantra, he should say: *tatsaviturvṛṇīmahe, sūryo devasya dhīmahi, bhargo devasya dhīmahi, dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt; so 'ham*.
Saying "saṃpracodayāt," he should silently give a staff made of *pālāśa* wood; then there is a feeding of Brahmins, then a feeding of Brahmins. (Kauthuma Gṛhyasūtra 17)

Having smeared each sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) a thousand times with all their limbs while reciting the *abhibhātmā* verses, and having made a bundle of sugarcane stalks and spread it out with the tips pointing north,

the teacher places the student upon it; then, placing a new winnowing basket on [the student’s] head and covering it with *kuśa* grass, the teacher fills his joined palms (*añjali*) with water from a jar.
Having stepped upon [the pupil] with his right foot, having recited the mantra "yena devā," having consecrated him with the mantra "eto nv indra," and having again clothed him in a garment,

he should smear a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), making it sloped toward the east as in the previous initiation (*upanayana*). Then, having filled that mound with either rice or barley according to his means, and having placed the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) upon it, the pupil is seated there in the same manner.

One should sprinkle milk and other substances upon the head of the disciple with the previously mentioned mantra. Having smeared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and performed the *praṇayana* rite as in the previous initiation (*upāyana*), the preceptor ties a triple-twisted girdle (*mekhalā*) around him. The disciple, having been made to recite the mantra silently, puts on the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) with the prescribed mantra. Then, having cleansed the shallow vessel (*śarāva*), he recites the verse "śanno devīḥ" and the five hundred *pāvamānī* verses.

Having purified [the area] three hundred times with "eto nū indra," eight hundred and forty times with "samāṃ," one hundred times with "śatavāraṇapraṇava," and one hundred and eight times with these [mantras], and having again performed the purification as previously described, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in a clean place,
take one thousand blades of *kuśa* grass— or two hundred and fifty— and dividing them into hundreds, one should place one hundred at the head and [another] hundred...

Having placed [the earth] under his feet and treading upon it, he should bind [the knots] one hundred each on both sides; having murmured "āpo hi ṣṭhā" a thousand times over his chest, "śanno devīḥ" twice that number, "eto nv indram" forty times, the Gāyatra [Sāman] five thousand times, and the Praṇava ten thousand times, he should complete the rite. (Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra 18)
Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra 19:
Now we shall explain the rule for the *aupāsana* fire.

When no specific time is prescribed, [the sacrifice] begins with the evening oblation and continues until the morning; they say that one attains splendor by performing the evening [oblation], provided one combines them.

Because it has been performed and because it was not [previously] attained, they say: "This is that which occurred here previously, according to what was attained. Therefore, there is attainment at the proper time; by day, from one watch (yāma) onwards, as has been stated, there is attainment. Therefore, there is non-attainment. Having recited the mantra over the water, having taken it up again, having consecrated it once with the *praṇava*, having drunk it and sipped water, and having immersed oneself in water to the depth of a finger's breadth, one should perform a thousand breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*).

Having recited "āpo hi ṣṭhā" one hundred times, "śanno devīḥ" two hundred times, "pāvamānīḥ" three hundred times, "eto nv indram" fourteen times, the *gāyatrī* fifteen times, and a thousand *praṇavas*—these are the eight; having recited these with a devout mind and standing in water up to the navel, one should perform a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāmas*) and then [recite] "āpo hi ṣṭhā" one hundred times. (KauthGS 19)
Kauthuma Gṛhyasūtra 20:
Now we shall explain the rule for the renewed student life (*punarbrahmacarya*).
Having subsisted on milk for six months and having entered the ocean, he performs the *nāndīmukha* rite as before; then follows the shaving of the head.

Having had eight [vessels] prepared and having appointed eight Brahmins, and having filled the eight earthen vessels with curds, honey, clarified butter, milk, sugar-water, coconut water, wine, and Ganges water, and having wrapped them in new cloth, he should consecrate the vessel of milk with the mantra "ā pyāyasva," the vessel of curds with "dadhi krāviṇa," the vessel of clarified butter with "śukram asi," and the vessel of honey with "madhu dhu cun dhanam."
With the verse "āpo hi ṣṭhā," he places pebbles; with "kayā naś citra," a coconut; with "gāyatre," cow’s urine; and with "evaṃ deva," a vessel of water mixed with flour. (Kauthuma Gṛhya Sūtra 20)
Kauthuma Gṛhyasūtra 21:

He should recite aloud, "Iti ete vā vām," while looking at the water to the right toward the sun; if he is unable [to look at the sun], he should do so once every watch, or at the end of a ghaṭikā, until sunset. Then, having performed the evening purification, he should take water in his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
Having taken [the water], he should enter the hut.

Sitting facing the east, he should then drink the water, wash his eyes, and perform the ritual sipping (ācamana). Then, he should recite the six verses that are the *devavrata* hymns: the two *prāṇāpāna*, the two *tavaśyāvīya*, the two *rājanaśāśāhin*, the two *gavāṃ vrata*, and "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ."
Furthermore, the repeated practice of these consists of fasting for twelve nights, neither remaining seated nor lying down, and not sleeping at all;
indeed, according to others, one does not even ask for alms during this vow.
One should not eat for twelve nights—having performed the fast in this manner for twelve nights, it is remembered as the *atikṛcchra*.
As long as Bṛhaspati is the Brahmā, so long is he glorified in the heavenly world; and he does not return again, and he does not return again. // KauthGS 21 //
The Kauthuma Gṛhyasūtra is completed.
